NEW YORK (CNN) -- Former New York City police Commissioner Bernard Kerik pleaded not guilty in federal court Monday to a revised indictment charging him in a corruption and tax evasion case, according to a spokesman for the New York District Attorney. A revised indictment brings to 15 the number of counts against former police Commissioner Bernard Kerik. The revised indictment includes two new counts of aiding the filing of false returns and a charge involving making false statements while applying for a housing loan, spokesman Herbert Hadad of the district attorney's office told CNN. Kerik is accused of failing to report more than $500,000 in income between 1999 and 2004, said Patricia Haynes, the IRS agent in charge of the case. Prosecutors allege Kerik received and concealed benefits of about $255,000 in renovations to his Riverdale, New York, apartment from a company seeking to do business with the city of New York. Revisions to the original indictment, which included charges of corruption, conspiracy and tax evasion, bring to 15 the number of counts against Kerik. Barry Berke, Kerik's attorney, declined to comment. The indictment also charges that Kerik made several false statements to the White House and other federal officials when he applied for the position as adviser to the Homeland Security Advisory Council, to the Coalition Provisional Authority in Iraq and in connection with his nomination to be secretary of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. U.S. District Judge Stephen Robinson did not rule Monday on whether the two counts that include charges of lying to White House officials will be tried in Washington or White Plains, New York. Kerik is due back in court February 3 for a hearing on pretrial motions, Hadad said. A trial date has not been set. Kerik, 53, is a longtime friend and former protege of former Mayor Rudy Giuliani. President Bush nominated him to be secretary of homeland security after winning re-election in 2004, but Kerik withdrew his name amid allegations that he employed a nanny who had a questionable immigration status. Bronx District Attorney Robert Johnson began investigating allegations that Kerik had traded payment on repairs to his Bronx apartment for favors, including city contracts. The former chief pleaded guilty in 2006 to accepting tens of thousands of dollars in gifts while he worked as city corrections commissioner. He was fined $221,000 and avoided jail time under his plea agreement. Before tapping Kerik for a Cabinet post, Bush dispatched him to Baghdad to train Iraqi police after the U.S. invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein. He left three months into an expected six-month stint, with Iraqi officials telling reporters that he had completed his assignment. In 2004, he campaigned for Bush's re-election and spoke at the Republican National Convention in New York. CNN's Mary Snow contributed to this report.

Kerik, who led the nation's largest police department during one of its most challenging periods, entered a plea of not guilty to the superseding indictment, which prosecutors said clarified and strengthened charges related to accusations that he accepted improper benefits and lied to government officials.

Standing before the judge, the former commissioner maintained his composure as the expanded counts were formally entered into the record.

His attorneys argued that the superseding indictment represented an effort to bolster a case they contended was fundamentally flawed. Prosecutors countered that the revisions provided greater specificity regarding the alleged pattern of conduct, and that the evidence supported each count.

The judge set a schedule for pretrial motions and future proceedings, with defense counsel indicating they intended to challenge several aspects of the government's case.

## The Charges

The indictment centered on allegations that Kerik accepted valuable benefits, including renovations to his residence, from parties seeking to do business with the city, and that he subsequently made false statements to government officials, including during the vetting process for federal positions.

Central to the government's case were accusations involving tax matters and false statements. Prosecutors alleged that Kerik failed to properly report income and benefits, and that he misled officials who were evaluating him for high-ranking government service.

The revised charges knit together allegations spanning his tenure in city government and his later interactions with federal authorities, presenting what prosecutors described as a sustained effort to conceal improper financial arrangements.

## A Meteoric Rise

Kerik's trajectory from working-class origins to the highest ranks of American law enforcement was, for a time, one of the most celebrated success stories in New York City politics.

Beginning his career in corrections, Kerik developed a close relationship with Rudolph Giuliani, working on Giuliani's mayoral campaign before ascending through city government. He was appointed Commissioner of the Department of Correction before Giuliani named him Police Commissioner in 2000.

His tenure as Police Commissioner coincided with the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. Images of Kerik at the World Trade Center site, coordinating the response alongside Giuliani, cemented his public image as a resolute leader during crisis. That reputation propelled him onto the national stage.

In 2004, President George W. Bush nominated Kerik to serve as Secretary of Homeland Security, a position that would have placed him in charge of the sprawling federal agency created in the aftermath of the attacks. The nomination represented the pinnacle of his public career.

The Homeland Security nomination proved to be the beginning of Kerik's downfall. Within days, questions emerged about his background, finances, and personal conduct. He withdrew his nomination, initially citing issues related to the employment of a household worker.

## History of Allegations

Additional questions touched on his conduct while overseeing city agencies, his personal relationships, and the accuracy of statements he provided to various officials over the course of his career.

The matters wound through both state and federal proceedings. At the state level, Kerik previously entered pleas related to certain allegations, acknowledging conduct in connection with benefits he had received. Those earlier proceedings foreshadowed the more serious federal case that would follow.

## The Broader Context

The case against Kerik drew significant public attention because of his prominence and the dramatic arc of his career. For many, his story represented a cautionary tale about the gap between public reputation and private conduct.

His defenders maintained that Kerik was a dedicated public servant whose genuine contributions during a period of national crisis were being overshadowed by the legal proceedings. They argued that the aggressive pursuit of the case reflected the scrutiny that comes with public prominence.

Critics and prosecutors, however, contended that Kerik had betrayed the public trust, using his positions of authority for personal benefit while concealing his conduct from the officials and institutions responsible for oversight.

## Looking Ahead

The revised indictment set the stage for continued legal proceedings that promised to keep Kerik's case in the public eye. With pretrial motions anticipated and a trial schedule to be determined, the former commissioner faced the prospect of a prolonged legal battle.

For a man who once stood at the summit of American law enforcement, the courtroom appearance marked another chapter in a remarkable fall from grace — a journey from national hero to federal defendant that captured the attention of a city and a nation that had once celebrated his rise.
